output.title: The quiet cost of overconfidence in one workflow
output.body:
Overconfidence is usually quiet. It lives in a process that feels familiar, so nobody stops to ask whether it is actually clean, fast, or safe. The cost shows up later as rework, missed approvals, duplicate entries, or a problem that only appears after it has moved downstream.

For a small business owner, the bounded question is not “use AI everywhere.” It is: what is the one repeatable workflow I keep treating as fine without measuring it? If a task is manual, repeated, and has a visible failure mode, it may be worth checking whether a small automation fits. If it is rare, sensitive, or depends on judgment, manual work can still be the better call.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach starts there. Identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and define scope, measures, and limits before anything is built. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. That is not a workaround; it is the control.

The practical next step is simple: name the single repeating task that creates the most rework or approval chasing, then decide whether it should stay manual or be checked for a bounded automation. Most founders only see the quiet cost once they measure it.
